title: Episode 3 (lines 589–736)

teacherSummary.text: Haemon, Creon's son and Antigone's betrothed, at first speaks respectfully, then urges his father to listen: the city secretly sympathizes with Antigone, and a wise man bends. Creon refuses; the argument grows bitter and Haemon leaves. Creon spares Ismene and sentences Antigone to be shut in a rock-hewn cave with a little food.

context.history: In Athens, ideas about rule by one man were debated openly; Haemon's "A State for one man is no State at all" (line 692) speaks to that debate.

significance: The image of trees that bend in a flood (lines 667–669) states the play's lesson that Creon learns too late.

satQuestions.passage:
Well spoken: so right-minded sons should feel,
In all deferring to a father’s will.
For ’tis the hope of parents they may rear
A brood of sons submissive, keen to avenge
Their father’s wrongs, and count his friends their own.
But who begets unprofitable sons,
He verily breeds trouble for himself,
And for his foes much laughter. Son, be warned
And let no woman fool away thy wits.
Ill fares the husband mated with a shrew,
And her embraces very soon wax cold.
For what can wound so surely to the quick
As a false friend? So spue and cast her off,
Bid her go find a husband with the dead.

anchorPassages.note: Absolute obedience doctrine that the play will overturn; gendered fear of being matched by a woman.
anchorPassages.text:
But he who overbears the laws, or thinks
To overrule his rulers, such an one
I never will allow. Whome’er the State
Appoints must be obeyed in everything,
Both small and great, just and unjust alike.
I warrant such an one in either case
Would shine, as King or subject; such a man
Would in the storm of battle stand his ground,
A comrade leal and true; but Anarchy—
What evils are not wrought by Anarchy!
She ruins States, and overthrows the home,
She dissipates and routs the embattled host;
While discipline preserves the ordered ranks.
Therefore we must maintain authority
And yield no tittle to a woman’s will.
Better, if needs be, men should cast us out
Than hear it said, a woman proved his match.

locator.opening: But he who overbears the laws, or thinks
locator.closing: hear it said, a woman proved his match.
locator.landmark: Creon on Anarchy: obey rulers in small and great, just and unjust; yield no tittle to a woman

anchorPassages.note: Teaching hinge: filial counsel and public murmur against a father's locked will.
anchorPassages.text:
Father, the gods implant in mortal men
Reason, the choicest gift bestowed by heaven.
’Tis not for me to say thou errest, nor
Would I arraign thy wisdom, if I could;
And yet wise thoughts may come to other men
And, as thy son, it falls to me to mark
The acts, the words, the comments of the crowd.
The commons stand in terror of thy frown,
And dare not utter aught that might offend,
But I can overhear their muttered plaints,
Know how the people mourn this maiden doomed
For noblest deeds to die the worst of deaths.
When her own brother slain in battle lay
Unsepulchred, she suffered not his corse
To lie for carrion birds and dogs to maul:
Should not her name (they cry) be writ in gold?
Such the low murmurings that reach my ear.
O father, nothing is by me more prized
Than thy well-being, for what higher good
Can children covet than their sire’s fair fame,
As fathers too take pride in glorious sons?
Therefore, my father, cling not to one mood,
And deem not thou art right, all others wrong.

locator.opening: Father, the gods implant in mortal men
locator.closing: deem not thou art right, all others wrong.
locator.landmark: Haemon: the people mourn Antigone; cling not to one mood; do not deem thyself alone right

anchorPassages.note: Practical wisdom: flexibility saves; rigid sail and root alike wreck in the gale.
anchorPassages.text:
For whoso thinks that wisdom dwells with him,
That he alone can speak or think aright,
Such oracles are empty breath when tried.
The wisest man will let himself be swayed
By others’ wisdom and relax in time.
See how the trees beside a stream in flood
Save, if they yield to force, each spray unharmed,
But by resisting perish root and branch.
The mariner who keeps his mainsheet taut,
And will not slacken in the gale, is like
To sail with thwarts reversed, keel uppermost.
Relent then and repent thee of thy wrath;
For, if one young in years may claim some sense,
I’ll say ’tis best of all to be endowed
With absolute wisdom; but, if that’s denied,
(And nature takes not readily that ply)
Next wise is he who lists to sage advice.

locator.opening: For whoso thinks that wisdom dwells with him,
locator.closing: wise is he who lists to sage advice.
locator.landmark: Haemon's yield-images: trees in flood, taut mainsheet; next wise is he who lists to advice

anchorPassages.note: Political core: Creon's one-man State answered by Haemon's desert-monarch jab.
anchorPassages.text:
What, shall the mob dictate my policy?
’Tis thou, methinks, who speakest like a boy.
Am I to rule for others, or myself?
A State for one man is no State at all.
The State is his who rules it, so ’tis held.
As monarch of a desert thou wouldst shine.
This boy, methinks, maintains the woman’s cause.
If thou be’st woman, yes. My thought’s for thee.
O reprobate, would’st wrangle with thy sire?
Because I see thee wrongfully perverse.
And am I wrong, if I maintain my rights?
Talk not of rights; thou spurn’st the due of Heaven.
O heart corrupt, a woman’s minion thou!
Slave to dishonour thou wilt never find me.
Thy speech at least was all a plea for her.
And thee and me, and for the gods below.
Living the maid shall never be thy bride.
So she shall die, but one will die with her.
Hast come to such a pass as threaten me?
What threat is this, vain counsels to reprove?
Vain fool to instruct thy betters; thou shalt rue it.
Wert not my father, I had said thou err’st.
Play not the spaniel, thou a woman’s slave.
When thou dost speak, must no man make reply?
This passes bounds. By heaven, thou shalt not rate
And jeer and flout me with impunity.
Off with the hateful thing that she may die
At once, beside her bridegroom, in his sight.

locator.opening: What, shall the mob dictate my policy?
locator.closing: At once, beside her bridegroom, in his sight.
locator.landmark: Clash: Shall the mob dictate? A State for one man is no State; desert-king taunt

anchorPassages.note: Living tomb: punishment that mirrors and perverts the burial rite she performed.
anchorPassages.text:
Surely, thou meanest not to slay them both?
I stand corrected; only her who touched
The body.
And what death is she to die?
She shall be taken to some desert place
By man untrod, and in a rock-hewn cave,
With food no more than to avoid the taint
That homicide might bring on all the State,
Buried alive. There let her call in aid
The King of Death, the one god she reveres,
Or learn too late a lesson learnt at last:
’Tis labour lost, to reverence the dead.

locator.opening: Surely, thou meanest not to slay them both?
locator.closing: ’Tis labour lost, to reverence the dead.
locator.landmark: Creon sentences Antigone to a rock-hewn cave with scant food, buried alive

weDoAnswers: In Athens, ideas about rule by one man were debated openly; Haemon's "A State for one man is no State at all" (line 692) speaks to that debate. Read closely: “See how the trees beside a stream in flood Save, if they yield to force, each spray unharmed, But by resisting perish root and branch.” (Haemon, lines 667–669).
analysis.weDoWords: “Yield”, “unharmed” and “perish root and branch” stand out in lines 667–669. Trees that bend in a flood survive, and trees that resist are destroyed, so Haemon urges his father to give way before it is too late. The wording makes stubbornness look like a root that can be torn up.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Therefore, my father, cling not to one mood, / And deem not thou art right, all others wrong” slowly and put it in my own words: Haemon asks his father not to lock himself into a single mood or to assume that only he is right. Next, craft. “Cling not to one mood” makes stubbornness sound like a grip, and “thou art right, all others wrong” exposes the isolation of that grip in four plain words. The strongest word is “cling”: it makes the father’s one mood sound like a grip he will not loosen. Then, effect. What do lines 660–661 reveal about Haemon and his father? My answer: Haemon is still speaking as a son, but he is already warning the king. The trees that bend in a flood (lines 667–669) state the lesson Creon will not take in time.

items.text: Why does Creon grow angrier as Haemon argues?
items.lookFor: He hears his son’s advice as a challenge to his authority, with evidence from the quarrel.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Creon hears Haemon’s counsel as a challenge to his rule, not as advice. He asks whether “the mob” shall dictate policy and whether he is “to rule for others, or myself” (lines 689–691), calls his son “a woman’s minion” (line 701), and finally threatens Antigone’s death “beside her bridegroom, in his sight” (lines 715–716). The anger rises because the son’s argument threatens the king’s authority.

It can also argue disloyalty: he tells Creon “A State for one man is no State at all” (line 692) and that Creon “spurn’st the due of Heaven” (line 700). The best answers show that Haemon claims loyalty while opposing the edict.
